narrative.summary: In the cold winter at Ashford Manor, during the circus troupe’s stay, Cecil Thorne is found stabbed in his locked room. The room appears sealed with no sign of forced entry or exit, and suspicion falls on the circus strongman Ivor Yardley. A cleverly concealed rotating wall panel allowed the murderer to enter and leave unseen, exploiting the manor’s secret architecture. Detective Adela Halloway uncovers the spatial deception through physical clues and social interactions, revealing the truth hidden beneath the manor’s façade.

accepted_facts: Cecil Thorne was found stabbed in his locked room at approximately quarter to ten.
The door and windows of the victim’s room were locked and bolted from the inside.
A heavy dagger was the murder weapon, missing from the manor’s weapon cabinet.
A faint metal pivot pin and unusual wear marks were observed on the carpet near the east wall of the victim’s room.
The manor has known secret passages and architectural quirks.
Ivor Yardley had a motive to kill Cecil and was seen near the stables rehearsal room shortly before the murder.
The room’s decorative moulding around one wall section was slightly misaligned.
Harriet Bellamy and Marguerite Selwyn had no access to the victim’s room during the murder window.
Ottoline Fairweather was in the drawing room during the murder window.
Adela Halloway observed the rotating panel mechanism during her inspection.
inferred_conclusions: The murder weapon was taken from the manor’s weapon cabinet and carried into the victim’s room.
The murderer used a rotating wall panel concealed beneath the carpet to enter and exit the locked room unnoticed.
Ivor Yardley could reach the weapon cabinet and the victim’s room via the secret panel.
The spatial illusion created by the rotating wall panel misled all witnesses about the murderer's true location.
The misaligned moulding and carpet wear are physical traces of the rotating panel’s use.
Ivor Yardley’s alibi does not cover the actual time of death due to the hidden access route.

mechanism.description: A large stone wall panel in the victim’s room rotates on a concealed pivot beneath a thick carpet, aligning a hidden doorway to the servants’ corridor. This allows entry and exit while the room appears sealed with locked door and windows. The rotating panel’s pivot is marked by a faint metal pin visible under the carpet edge. The panel’s movement causes unusual wear on the carpet and disrupts the decorative moulding alignment. The culprit used this mechanism to enter the victim’s room undetected, commit the murder using a dagger taken from the manor’s weapon cabinet, and exit before the room was discovered locked and sealed.

delivery_path.step: The culprit takes the dagger from the weapon cabinet in the servants’ quarters.
Using knowledge of the secret rotating wall panel, the culprit enters the victim’s locked room unseen.
The culprit stabs the victim with the dagger to the heart.
The culprit exits through the rotating panel, returning it to its original position to maintain the illusion of a sealed room.
The locked door and windows remain undisturbed, confusing investigators.

outcome.result: The rotating wall panel allowed the murderer to commit the crime within a seemingly impossible sealed room scenario, deceiving all observers until the spatial illusion was uncovered by detective Adela Halloway.

false_assumption.statement: The victim’s room was completely sealed and inaccessible except through the locked door and windows.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: All doors and windows were locked and bolted from the inside, and no footprints or forced entry signs were found.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: A concealed rotating wall panel provided hidden access to the room, invalidating the assumption that the room was completely sealed.

supporting_points: Marguerite was seen near the manor corridors shortly before the murder and had a tense relationship with the victim.
Her alibi is weaker than others, and she was present in the manor during the relevant time window.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The rotating wall panel’s physical traces do not align with Marguerite’s access or opportunity, and the dagger’s handling marks do not match her gloves.

red_herrings.description: Dagger glove mark found in the drawing room, belonging to Ottoline Fairweather.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: Ottoline handled the dagger earlier during a display and left glove marks unrelated to the murder.

red_herrings.description: Suspicious footprints near the window of the victim’s room.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: The footprints were from a staff member delivering food earlier that evening before the room was locked.

closed_circle.rationale: The manor was isolated by fog and frost; no outsiders could enter unnoticed. All suspects were accounted for within the estate during the murder window.

discriminating_test.design: Recreate the victim’s room setup with the carpet lifted and the rotating wall panel manipulated to demonstrate entry and exit paths. Measure the time required to rotate the panel and pass through it, comparing it to Ivor Yardley’s alibi and known movements. Use the stopped clock’s time to prove the discrepancy between the apparent and actual time of death, thus exposing the spatial illusion and confirming Ivor’s access during the murder window.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The test confirms the physical possibility and timing of the rotating panel’s use and the false clock setting, disproving the sealed-room assumption and implicating Ivor Yardley.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The rotating panel’s operation time fits within Ivor Yardley’s unaccounted window and the clock discrepancy invalidates his claimed alibi.

fair_play.explanation: Step 1: The dagger’s handling mark in the servants’ corridor and access permissions clarify who could move the murder weapon. Step 2: The physical evidence of the rotating panel’s pivot pin and carpet wear reveal the hidden access. Step 3: Witness sightings and alibis combined with known panel existence narrow the suspect pool to Ivor Yardley. Step 4: The stopped clock’s actual time exposes the false timeline, confirming the spatial deception. All these clues are presented before the discriminating test, allowing the reader to logically deduce the culprit.
